extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and religious experience (e.g., undergraduates, graduate students, and academic readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for constructing and judging metaphysical and philosophical hypotheses about consciousness, pluralism vs monism, and the role of religious/psychical data. Emphasizes empirical thickening, pragmatic belief-formation, and practical consequences of theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider religious experiences as distinct empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: There are religious experiences of a specific nature, not deducible by analogy or psychological reasoning from our other sorts of experience; they point with reasonable probability to the continuity of our consciousness with a wider spiritual environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James urges that such 'experiences of an unexpected life succeeding upon death' be 'carefully considered and interpreted by every one who aspires to reason out a more complete philosophy.' He treats them as discontinuous with ordinary experience and as direct empirical evidence that should be admitted alongside other data (psychology, psychical research) when forming metaphysical views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden and 'thicken' the empirical basis of philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is high time for the basis of discussion in these questions to be broadened and thickened up.' Philosophy should take into account the particulars of life rather than rely only on thin logical abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely, James recommends drawing on Fechner, Bergson, descriptive psychology, religious experiences, and psychical research to build probabilistic, empirically informed pictures of superhuman consciousness. He urges philosophers to 'imitate the sciences' by incorporating richer empirical analogies and facts into theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monistic dogmatism; favour compromise, mediation, and pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Compromise and mediation are inseparable from the pluralistic philosophy.' Monistic dogmatism is criticised as saying 'It is either that or nothing; take it or leave it just as it stands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James argues that philosophers should be open to pluralistic hypotheses (finite, multiple consciousnesses, Fechnerian 'earth-souls') rather than insisting on an all-encompassing absolute. He treats pluralism as a fully co-ordinate hypothesis with monism and encourages readiness to make empirically grounded compromises between experience and abstract theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge metaphysical views by their fit with immediate empirical experience ('each-form')
rubrics_metrics.description: Pluralism pragmatically means that the sundry parts of reality may be externally related; 'nothing real is absolutely simple... a bit of reality when actively engaged in one of these relations is not by that very fact engaged in all the other relations simultaneously.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James suggests the standard that metaphysical hypotheses should cohere with the structure of immediate (concrete) experience—the 'each-form'—where parts have mediated connexions and continuity is of the 'strung-along' type rather than instantaneous co-implication. Theories that better mirror such empirical features are favoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear evaluative concepts (foreignness vs intimacy) over ambiguous appeals to 'rationality'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'rational' carries too many meanings; better to use 'foreignness' and 'intimacy' to express contrasts between monism and pluralism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of fighting over whose definition of 'rational' wins, assess theories by whether they make the universe feel 'intimate' (pluralism) or 'foreign' (monism) to human experience. This is a methodological recommendation for clearer, more relevant evaluative vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow pragmatic (non‑logical) grounds for adopting hypotheses ('will to believe' / 'faith-ladder')
rubrics_metrics.description: James describes a 'faith-ladder' in which a conception that 'is not self-contradictory' may progress from 'it might be true' to 'it shall be held for true' for the individual—'Not one step in this process is logical, yet it is the way in which monists and pluralists alike espouse and hold fast to their visions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He treats practical-political or affective readiness to adopt a hypothesis as a legitimate factor in belief-formation, especially where the hypothesis is live, momentous, and not decidable by logic alone. This legitimises pragmatic commitment as part of methodological choice-making in philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate theories by their practical consequences and reciprocal influence on action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Our thoughts determine our acts, and our acts redetermine the previous nature of the world.' Philosophies are intimate parts of the universe and alter the 'current of being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James advises assessing philosophical systems partly by their effects in practice: do they enable life, action, and repair of the world (pluralism's self-reparative aspect)? Theories that generate beneficial practical consequences and allow human agency in shaping reality are methodologically preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept empirical risk (superstitions etc.) but do not let fear deter inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: If belief in higher consciousnesses or psychical phenomena grows orthodox, 'superstitions and wild-growing over-beliefs' will abound; 'still more will they superabound... But ought one seriously to allow such a timid consideration as that to deter one from following the evident path of greatest religious promise?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James recommends a risk-balanced stance: pursue empirical investigation of religious/psychical claims despite the likelihood of false positives and social excesses, because the potential religious and philosophical gains justify the search. He frames this as a pragmatic methodological choice, not a purely epistemic one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat pluralism as a self-reparative hypothesis involving human contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The incompleteness of the pluralistic universe is 'self-reparative through us, as getting its disconnections remedied in part by our behavior'—'We use what we are and have, to know; and what we know, to be and have still more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, prefer hypotheses that allow for human participation in completing or improving the world; this circular relation between knowledge and being is an evaluative feature favouring pluralistic accounts that incorporate agency and historical development.
